after.commitMessage:
feat: MAKEZERO number-match puzzle

Board of 1-9 tiles, nine to a row. A selection clears when it is two tiles
showing the same number, or when two to five tiles add up to ten. Tiles link
by 8-way grid adjacency or by reading order once cleared squares are skipped,
and a chain only has to connect step by step.

Longer chains are much harder to spot, so the reward curve is steep:
10 / 30 / 70 / 150 points for two / three / four / five tiles.

Tap to build a chain step by step (it settles as soon as it is legal), or drag
across tiles and lift to commit. Fully cleared rows drop out. The + action
copies the surviving numbers onto the end of the board to break a deadlock,
and the hint action points at one legal chain; both are limited.

Game rules live in src/game as pure functions with 38 tests; src/ui holds the
DOM renderer, pointer handling, and per-day best score.

before.commitMessage:
feat: package MAKEZERO as an Android app for Play

Wraps the web build with Capacitor 8, which already defaults to
compileSdk/targetSdk 36 — the level Google Play requires of new apps from
2026-08-31.

- portrait-locked activity, wood-coloured launch theme so start never flashes
  white, and the stretched splash bitmaps dropped for the Android 12+ splash API
- adaptive and legacy launcher icons generated from the game's own tile art,
  replacing the default template vectors
- release signing reads android/keystore.properties, which stays untracked
  alongside the keystore itself
- CI runs tests, typecheck and a debug APK build; a manual workflow produces the
  signed .aab for anyone without a local Android SDK
- store/ carries the 512 icon, 1024x500 feature graphic and two phone
  screenshots captured from the running game
- README documents the rules, the keystore steps and the Play Console checklist

The .aab could not be built in this container: its network policy blocks
dl.google.com, so the Android SDK cannot be fetched here. The CI workflow
covers that build.

after.commitMessage:
feat: story, time attack and endless modes

Splits what varies between modes into a RunConfig — starting rows, adds,
hints, spawn weights, and an optional clock — so the matching rules stay
untouched and only the goal and resources change.

Story: 20 stages in 4 chapters of 5. Clear the whole board within the stage's
add budget. Three dials tighten together — adds 8 to 2, rows 3 to 7, and a
spawn table leaning on the hard-to-pair 7/8/9 — interpolated so each one hits
its extreme at the final stage rather than plateauing partway. Clearing a
chapter's last stage plays its story beat.

Time attack: 60 seconds. A deadlock is topped up with the survivors and a
board cleared outright is redealt, so the run never stalls; only the clock
ends it.

Endless: unchanged.

Chapters live in story.ts as data — image path, name and lines — and the art
in public/story/ is placeholder work meant to be overwritten in place.

solver.test.ts plays every stage with a greedy bot across 12 fixed seeds. It
caught the original curve flattening after stage 14, and now guards that no
stage is unclearable and that difficulty still climbs to the end.

Tile rendering and pointer gestures move to boardView.ts so the controller is
only screens and HUD. 61 unit tests, plus a browser pass over all three modes
and the chapter beat.

before.commitMessage:
feat: sum-to-ten only, line of sight, fixed board

Removes same-number matching. A selection now clears only when two to five
tiles add up to exactly ten; repeated values inside a chain (1+1+8) are still
fine. Connection becomes a single rule — a straight line, horizontal, vertical
or diagonal, with no surviving tile in the way — replacing grid adjacency plus
the reading-order wrap that read as arbitrary on screen.

Three things had to change with it, each because simulation said so:

Boards are dealt as groups that already sum to ten rather than loose random
numbers. Every clear removes exactly ten, so the total's last digit never
changes; a random board is unclearable nine times in ten, and simulated runs
failed all 120 games with the board growing past 490 tiles.

The + action becomes a shuffle. Copying the survivors duplicated whatever the
player was stuck on — without same-number matching nothing broke the loop, and
leftovers climbed from 8 to 355 as more copies were spent. Shuffling keeps the
numbers and only moves them, so the board never grows.

Stage goals become star grades. A perfect clear turned out to depend on the
deal, not the player: on two of three sampled boards, 120 randomised
playthroughs never got below three tiles. Stars are scored on tiles left, with
targets set as a share of the board that tightens each stage.

The deal's group sizes work backwards from the obvious reading, so the comments
say so: many large groups make a board easier, since five values totalling ten
average two apiece and small numbers combine freely. Plain pairs spread the
values out and strand the rigid 8s and 9s.

The board is dealt at a fixed size and never grows, so it is laid out to fit
the screen — 5x8 at stage 1 up to 10x15 at stage 20, tiles sized to the space
available. Nothing scrolls, which leaves one-finger drag free for selection.

Greedy play now grades 2.42 stars at stage 1 falling to 0.92 at stage 20, every
stage passable. 70 unit tests, plus browser passes over the rules, the layout at
both board extremes, and all three modes.

after.commitMessage:
refactor: drop the position rule, reorganise into core/content/ui

Tiles may now be combined wherever they sit. A selection clears when two to
five surviving tiles add up to exactly ten, and nothing else is checked — no
adjacency, no straight line, no line of sight. That answers both reports:
1+1+1+7 totals ten and was only ever refused because the four tiles did not
share a line, and "nothing left to connect" fired while combinations were
still on the board.

The shuffle goes with it. Rearranging tiles cannot change a verdict that never
looks at position, so it had nothing left to do. A run now ends exactly when no
values on the board can make ten, which core/solver.ts answers from the nine
value counts rather than by walking the grid.

Two selection fixes this exposed: a tile that would push the running total past
ten now starts a fresh selection instead of piling onto an unclearable heap,
and tapping the board outside any tile abandons the selection.

Structure, since this will keep being edited:

  src/core/     rules engine — no DOM, fully tested
  src/content/  stage curve, star targets, chapters and lines
  src/ui/       screens, split into title / hud / overlay / story
  docs/         why it is built this way

Dependencies run one way, ui -> content -> core, so a skin change never reaches
the rules. The stylesheet is split to match, with the palette in tokens.css.

docs/DECISIONS.md records the findings that are counter-intuitive enough to be
undone by accident: random boards are mathematically unclearable because each
clear removes exactly ten and never changes the total's last digit; dealing
many large groups makes a board easier rather than harder; a perfect clear
depends on the deal, so three stars is a small number rather than an empty
board. Each entry carries the measurement behind it.

57 unit tests, plus browser passes over the rules, the layout at both board
extremes, all three modes and the chapter beat.

after.commitMessage:
feat: endless becomes a survival mode

Tiles now keep arriving in endless. The board is a fixed frame dealt about
half full, a batch lands every few seconds, and cleared squares stay open as
the room those batches land in — so the board neither grows nor collapses rows
the way a story stage does. The run ends when a batch has nowhere to go.

Batches are whole sum-to-ten groups, never loose tiles. Dropping singles would
bring back the problem that makes a random board unclearable: each clear
removes exactly ten, so the total's last digit never moves.

The gap between batches shortens as the run goes on, and that floor is the
whole mode. It has to sit just below how fast a person can actually play.
Simulated against a bot that clears every N milliseconds:

  floor 850ms   quick player 900s+ (never died)   slow player 107s
  floor 650ms   quick player  587s                slow player 101s
  floor 400ms   quick player   99s                slow player  62s

Too high and a quick player outruns the spawner forever; too low and the floor
kills everyone at the same rate, so playing well stops mattering. 650ms keeps a
casual run near two minutes while still paying for speed. pacing.test.ts
simulates the clock and guards both ends of that.

Two fixes this surfaced:

The board view held its own reference to the board, so tiles that arrived on a
timer rendered only after the player's next move. It now re-points at the
current board every render, keeping any half-built selection intact rather than
cancelling it when a batch lands.

A square nothing has ever stood on carries value 0 and renders blank. It was
showing a ghost 1 — the placeholder it was created with.

Docs updated: the endless section in RULES.md, the spawn dials and their
measurements in BALANCE.md, and the floor trade-off in DECISIONS.md.

after.commitMessage:
feat: hands-on tutorial and a personal records screen

The tutorial teaches by making the player do it: five boards, each for one
idea — a pair making ten, three tiles, the two 3s that look pairable but are
only six, a 9 and a 1 at opposite ends of the board, and a five-tile chain for
the 150. It opens on a first launch, can be skipped at any point, and is
replayable from the title.

Every tutorial board is built so exactly one combination adds up to ten, which
lets the game's own rules judge the answer. There is no second 'is this the
move I meant?' check to drift out of step with them, and tutorial.test.ts
enumerates every board to prove a second answer has not crept in. Boards may
still carry other tiles — those are the lesson, not noise.

The records screen collects what a player has to show for their time: best
time-attack and endless scores, the star earned on each of the twenty stages,
and the running total. Stage grades are stored per stage, keeping the best a
stage has ever earned.

Two smaller pieces this needed. BoardView takes an optional maximum tile size,
since a nine-tile teaching board would otherwise blow up to fill a phone
screen. Progress storage gained per-stage stars and a tutorial-seen flag, both
defaulted so an existing save loads unchanged.

78 unit tests, plus browser passes over the tutorial (wrong move refused, all
five steps, skip, replay, does not nag on the second launch) and the records
screen.

before.commitMessage:
fix: the board no longer clips or floats in a margin

Two layout bugs that only showed on a real phone.

The board was clipped. It sizes its tiles by measuring the room it has, and
that measurement ran before the HUD did — so it sized against a box that still
had the previous run's timer bar showing and a one-line notice, then the chrome
settled and the board no longer fitted. The HUD now renders first.

The board floated in a wide margin. The dark frame was on .board-wrap, which
stretches the full width, while the tiles are sized to fit both directions and
so end up narrower. The frame moves to .board, which is exactly the size of the
tiles it holds.

Refitting is now driven by a ResizeObserver rather than window.resize. The
window stays the same size while that box changes constantly — browser bars
sliding away, a notice wrapping to two lines, the keyboard, a foldable opening.
It is safe from feedback because .board-wrap takes its height from flex and
never from the board inside it.

On short screens the chrome gives up its room before the tiles do: header,
chips, timer and buttons shrink at 660px, and the notice goes at 520px. The
16px tile floor is a last resort, not the first move.

tests/browser/responsive.mjs is kept in the repo because unit tests cannot
reach any of this — a board sized by measurement needs a real browser at a real
size to verify. It checks ten devices plus rotation both ways for clipping,
page overflow and unusably small tiles. Playwright stays out of package.json;
the script says how to install it.

after.commitMessage:
feat: TAP to TEN — an 81-tile deck and a Broadway skin

Every stage now deals the same deck: nine of each digit, 81 tiles on a 9x9
board. The counts are the puzzle rather than a random draw, which makes the
game the same for everyone and finally testable end to end.

The deck has a property worth knowing before touching it. 81 is odd and 5 only
pairs with itself, so pairing everything away leaves exactly one tile, and it
is always a 5: the total is 405, every clear removes exactly ten, and that last
digit never moves. Three stars therefore means one tile left, not none.

Scoring becomes 10/20/40/80 — each extra tile doubles the reward. Chosen by
simulating the deck against several curves: clearing with pairs empties the
board to its last tile for 400, while chasing long chains tops out near 550 but
strands about 27 tiles. Stars reward the first and score the second, so a run
has to pick one. Spending 1s on a five-chain is what strands the 9s.

The look moves to a Broadway house — velvet, brass and marquee bulbs — with the
palette entirely in tokens.css. The board is anchored to the top and the room
below it is a stage floor for the dancer; art drops into #stage-floor and the
CSS stands it on the floor, centred. On a short screen that space yields first
and the board keeps its size.

Fixes a measurement bug the new frame exposed: getBoundingClientRect returns
the border box, so the frame's own border has to be subtracted along with its
padding, or a nine-wide board overshoots by two pixels.

Difficulty is now the hints and the star targets, since the deck is fixed. That
also means every stage is mathematically the same puzzle — noted in
DECISIONS.md, along with what to change if stages should differ.

80 unit tests, layout checked across ten screens plus rotation, and the four
browser suites pass.

after.commitMessage:
feat: ninety-nine stages, and a story you are meant to finish empty

Story asks for the whole board now. A stage deals its numbers as groups
that each add to ten, so the deal always comes apart — checked exactly,
by search, at every checkpoint and every seed: 100%. What a player picks
is another matter. A clear that cuts across two groups strands tiles
nothing will ever match:

  1 2 3 4 6 7 8 9   comes apart as (1,9)(2,8)(3,7)(4,6)
  take 1+2+3+4 first and 6 7 8 9 is left with no ten in it

Measured over forty seeds a run: a line that takes any legal move
empties the board 35% of the time on stage 1 and 0% by stage 99; always
taking the longest combination, or always taking pairs, is near zero
throughout; a line that only makes moves keeping the board emptiable
gets there every time, on every stage. Being stuck is a mistake, and
never a fixed strategy's fault.

So a move can be taken back, and that is a resource rather than a
convenience — it is what makes "empty the board" a fair goal. It works
on a dead board too, which is the moment it matters, and the last stage
still carries one: at zero there is no way back from a mistake.

Stars follow: three for an empty board played unaided, two for an empty
board, one as consolation for coming close so a run never hard-locks.

The curve runs 1 to 99 over eleven chapters. Four rows to eleven, loose
groups to rigid pairs, five hints to none, five take-backs to one. The
dial is not size — it is how much a wrong move costs.

Also: five blocks that do not add to ten are refused where they stand.
There is no sixth to come, so the selection was already dead while it
sat there looking alive. The board sways and the five flash red before
they let go — a selection that merely vanished left the player unsure
the tap had registered.

after.commitMessage:
feat: a picture under every board, and a dealer that stops hoarding 1s

Story is a collection now. Each stage has a picture behind its board;
clearing a block turns that square transparent, so the picture arrives a
square at a time, and emptying the board is how it is kept. Ninety-nine
stages, ninety-nine pictures. Stars are gone — the goal is binary, and a
second reward on top of it only blurs which one you are playing for.

That has a consequence in the rules: story boards no longer collapse a
row when it empties. A row that closed up would drag the holes out of
line with the part of the picture they had uncovered.

The dealer was the other half. It used to pick a group size and then
roll digits, and five tiles that add to ten average two apiece, so a
board came out 55% 1s and 2s with a 9 on one tile in a hundred. Long
combinations then ate the small numbers and left 7s, 8s and 9s with
nothing to pair with — measured, the leftovers held no 1s or 2s at all.
It now picks whole groups from the thirty-odd that add to ten, choosing
each by what the board is still short of. 1s fall from 37% to 23% on the
first stage and 13% on the last; 9s rise from 1% to 8%. Scoring is per
tile rather than per group, or a group of five wins on term count alone
and the skew comes straight back.

That distribution also sets the group sizes, so the old dial is gone: a
board that wants few 1s deals mostly pairs without being told to.

New item: split a block into pieces that add to the same thing — a 5
becomes 3 and 2, or 1, 1, 1 and 2. Which is not the player's to choose.
The sum is preserved so the arithmetic cannot break, but a clear holds
at most five blocks, and splitting inside a group of four can leave a
group of six that no single clear can take. Every roll is checked
against an exact emptiability search and rolled again if it would
strand the board, so the promise that a story board can be emptied
survives the item. The pieces land in already-cleared squares, which
means a full board cannot be split and a split covers part of the
picture back up.

The opening distribution is the most sensitive number in the curve: a
slightly more level one drops a careless line's success on stage 1 from
30% to 8%. docs/BALANCE.md carries the measurements and says so.

after.commitMessage:
Give the board its room back, and put a choosing step in front of every mode (#9)

Three things, from the mockup pass and the screenshot that came with it.

The board had quietly shrunk to 68% of the screen. `.board-wrap` carried an
`aspect-ratio` while sitting on `flex: 0 1 auto`, so when the HUD grew the box
gave up height — and the ratio dragged its width down with it. The frame now
takes whatever room the chrome leaves and nothing more; how many tiles fit is
measured, not declared, so `--board-ratio` and the empty `#stage-floor` are
gone. Back to 92% on every screen in the layout suite.

"갤러리 보기" on the results panel threw instead of navigating: `result ->
gallery` was not an allowed transition, so the player was left staring at the
finished board. Opened, with a regression test.

And modes no longer start the instant they are tapped. Story runs ninety-nine
stages with a different picture behind each, which is worth seeing before
committing to one, so it goes through a chapter list, a 3x3 stage grid and a
card showing the picture (or `?`) and the time to beat. Time attack and endless

after.commitMessage:
Move to a paper skin, and pay time attack back for a good run (#14)

Three things.

The cover becomes cover2 — 4837x9540 in, a 1080x2130 WebP out at 253KB. Its
0.507 aspect is closer to a phone's than the old 0.447, so the `contain`
margins shrink with it. The old source is deleted.

The skin goes light, and the cover only confirmed the decision rather than
driving it. Clearing a block uncovers the picture hidden beneath, and those
pictures are toy renders on white — on a night-blue board every cleared square
opened as a glaring white hole, all the way to the end of the stage, which
undercuts the whole point of the mode. On paper the reveal is continuous.
Cream ground, maroon ink, the wordmark's orange and yellow for anything active.

The nine block colours are spaced around the wheel rather than chosen to
taste: the board is read in groups, so two confusable digits at 35px means the
eye beats the rules. 8 started as cyan, which put three blues on one board
next to 1 and 2, and is now chocolate — the one warm dark the paper carries.
The 81 hardcoded rgba values scattered through the screen files collapse into
--panel, --slab, --recess, --sheen and --scrim, so the next skin change is one
file rather than nine.

Time attack now pays for a good run, where before it only ran you out of tiles
faster. Every hundred points adds nine low tiles — nine is exactly one row on
a nine-wide board, and 1s, 2s and 3s are what long combinations are always
starved of, so it is fuel and not clutter. Five hundred buys thirty seconds
and a fresh board, once: a second extension would turn a good run endless,
which is the other mode. Both thresholds are read off the score rather than
remembered, which works because the mode has no take-backs, so nothing new is
stored. The HUD says what landed — a row appearing at the bottom of the board
is not something a player racing a clock notices on their own.

104 unit tests, layout, drag and feedback all green.

after.commitMessage:
Two modes, English throughout, a new cover, and a word at the end of a run (#16)

Story leaves the title screen; time attack and endless are the game now. The
chapters, stages and pictures stay in the code untouched, so bringing it back
is putting one button back. The gallery has no way to fill any more, but the
two mode records it also holds are still worth seeing, so it keeps its screen
under the name RECORDS.

Every string the player reads is English — buttons, notices, rules, the
tutorial, the story lines, and the browser suites' output with them. Plain
words throughout: "Clear every block to win the picture", "Make ten to score".

The cover becomes cover-3 and now fills the width on every phone rather than
fitting inside it. `contain` left the picture small on a tall screen; the
artwork carries white margins above and below precisely so the width can be
filled and the overflow cropped from margin rather than art. It is positioned
and translated rather than centred by an auto margin, because an auto margin
gives up and snaps to the top the moment the image is taller than the box —
which is the case that matters, and which cropped a short phone entirely from
the bottom.

A run now ends on a word before it ends on numbers: GOOD TRY, NICE, GREAT or
AMAZING by score, held 1.4 seconds. The last move and a panel of numbers
arriving together read as being marked rather than as having finished
something. The artwork behind the word is optional and off by default, so the
game never waits on an asset to look right — see docs/CONTENT.md.

The layout, drag and feedback suites walked through story to reach a board;
they now use time attack, which deals the same full nine-by-nine deck. Endless
was tried first and its sparse opening board made two checks meaningless.

104 unit tests, layout, drag and feedback all green.

after.commitMessage:
Call it TIMELESS, draw the take-back as a loop, and let sums climb (#34)

Three changes to the new mode.

**The name.** TIMELESS, in the code as well as on screen — `clearAll` becomes
`timeless` throughout, config and saved record included. The `MAKE 10 · 20 · 30`
line above the SUM box stays: that was never the name, it is the rule.

**The rule.** Landing exactly on ten clears there and then; stepping over it to
eleven means the selection is heading for twenty, and past twenty it heads for
thirty. Past thirty still busts. That makes the mode's own input rule
disappear: a selection was being held past ten only while the finger stayed
down, so a tap and a drag behaved differently. They behave the same now — what
you pick decides, not how you hold it — and the drag special case is gone.
Single-target modes were never affected either way.

**The icon.** The take-back arrow was rendering as a dark blob: the drawn
glyphs are outlines and nothing was saying so, so the browser filled the paths
in black. They are stroked in the button's own colour now, and the arrow is a
loop turning back on itself. The split icon was wrong the same way and is
fixed with it.

after.commitMessage:
Keep the page paper so Safari's bars never take the studio's orange (#49)

The orange was not in the page at all — it was iOS Safari's status bar and
address bar. Safari reads the page's colour once, at load, and neither a later
`theme-color` nor a later screen reaches the bars, so opening on the studio's
card left orange furniture around the game for the rest of the session.

So the page is paper from the first frame and stays paper. `theme-color` is
fixed in the markup and no longer touched by script — driving it was the wrong
instinct, and by this mechanism it would have made the orange permanent rather
than temporary. The root owns the page colour now instead of the body: on a
phone the app is shorter than the window, and the strips the browser paints
around it come from the root, which should not be resting on CSS's propagation
rule. The orange is painted on the studio card's own box, where Safari never
reads it.

Reproduced the condition rather than the device — the app held to 700px inside
an 852px window — and sampled the pixels outside it: paper on all three cards.

Also: the browser suites need CHROME_PATH in this environment and die without
it, which I had not noticed while writing "layout · drag · feedback all pass"
on recent pull requests. They were not run. Run properly, one was genuinely
broken, and by my own change: centring a lone tool with `display: none`
collapsed the whole action row in time attack, which carries no tools, and the
board there sat 32px off every other mode. Reserving the row's height fixed
that and cost the board its tiles in landscape. A hidden tool now gives up its
width — a negative margin cancels the flex gap it would still be given — and
keeps its height, so the lone tool still centres and the row is the same height
in every mode at every size, with no per-breakpoint numbers to keep in step.

Units 123 · layout 14 · drag 9 · feedback 9, all actually run.
